cue: Describe a rule that you disagree with.
closing: and explain why you disagree with it.
followUps: Have you ever broken this rule?
sampleAnswer: The rule I'd like to talk about is one that many schools in my country have, which is a complete ban on mobile phones during the school day. Students have to hand their phones in when they arrive in the morning, or keep them switched off in their lockers, and if a teacher sees a phone, it's confiscated until the end of the week. It was introduced by the regional education authority a few years ago, and individual schools have to enforce it. My younger brother is still at secondary school, so I hear about it quite a lot. Now, I should say that I understand the reasoning behind it. Phones can be a huge distraction, there have been problems with cyberbullying, and some teachers were frustrated that students were checking social media under their desks instead of paying attention. So I'm not arguing that students should be free to use their phones whenever they like. What I disagree with is the fact that it's a blanket ban with no exceptions. Phones are also incredibly useful learning tools. Students could use them to look up information, record experiments in science, or practise languages with apps, and banning them completely means teachers can't take advantage of any of that. More importantly, I think the rule misses an opportunity. These teenagers are going to spend their whole adult lives surrounded by technology, and school should be the place where they learn to use it responsibly, rather than a place where it simply disappears for seven hours. It's a bit like trying to teach people to swim by keeping them away from water. I'd much prefer a more flexible approach, where phones are allowed in certain lessons for specific tasks and switched off the rest of the time, with clear consequences for misuse. That would address the genuine problems without treating every student as if they couldn't be trusted.

topic: A time you changed your mind
cue: Describe a time when you changed your mind about something important.
bullets: what made you change your mind
how long it took you to change your mind
closing: and explain how you felt after changing your mind.
followUps: Do you find it easy to admit that you were wrong?
sampleAnswer: I'm going to talk about how I changed my mind about doing a gap year before university. When I was finishing school, I was absolutely convinced that taking a year off was a waste of time. Most of my friends were going straight to university, and I had this idea that anyone who took a gap year was either lazy or just putting off growing up. I'd been offered a place on an economics degree, and my plan was to start immediately, finish as soon as possible and get a job. What changed my mind was a combination of things, really. The first was a conversation with my cousin, who's a few years older than me. She'd spent a year working in a hostel in Ireland and then volunteering on a farm, and when she described it, she didn't sound lazy at all; she sounded more confident and much clearer about what she wanted than I was. That made me question my assumptions. The second thing was that, if I was honest with myself, I wasn't sure economics was right for me. I'd chosen it because it seemed sensible, not because I was excited about it. So it wasn't a sudden decision. It took me about three months of thinking, reading other people's experiences online and, I have to admit, quite a few arguments with my parents, who were worried I'd never go back to studying. In the end, I deferred my place and spent the year working in a café to save money and then travelling around South America for four months. When I came back, I actually changed my degree to geography, which I've loved. Changing my mind made me feel a bit embarrassed at first, because I'd been so outspoken about gap years being pointless. But looking back, I feel proud of it, because it taught me that holding a strong opinion isn't the same as being right, and that it's worth listening to people whose experience is different from yours.

cue: Describe a time when someone criticised you and it turned out to be helpful.
bullets: how you reacted at the time
closing: and explain why the criticism was helpful in the end.
followUps: Is it easier to accept criticism from friends or from strangers?
sampleAnswer: The example I'd like to give happened during my first job after university, when I was working as a junior analyst in a small consultancy. A few months after I started, I had to give a presentation to a client, and I'd spent days preparing it. I was quite pleased with myself, because I'd included a huge amount of data and analysis. Afterwards, my manager, a woman called Elena, took me aside and told me, quite bluntly, that the presentation had been a disaster. She said that I'd crammed far too much information onto every slide, that I'd spoken too fast, and that by the end the client had obviously stopped listening. Her exact words were something like, they don't need to know everything you know, they need to know what to do next. To be honest, my first reaction was defensive. I felt hurt, and I remember thinking she was being unfair, because I'd worked so hard. I went home that evening feeling quite sorry for myself and even wondering whether I was in the wrong job. But over the next few days, I calmed down and started to think about what she'd said, and I realised she was completely right. I'd been trying to prove how hard I'd worked, rather than trying to help the client. So I asked her if she'd give me some advice, and she spent an hour going through the slides with me and showing me how to focus on two or three key messages. The next presentation I gave went far better, and the client actually thanked me for being so clear. The reason the criticism was so helpful is that it changed the way I communicate in general, not just in presentations. I now always ask myself what my audience actually needs. It also taught me that the people who tell you uncomfortable truths are often the ones who care most about your progress.

topic: A time you had to be patient
cue: Describe a time when you had to be very patient.
bullets: what you were waiting for or dealing with
how you managed to stay patient
closing: and explain what you learned from the experience.
followUps: Do you think people today are less patient than in the past?
sampleAnswer: I'd like to talk about the year I spent learning to play the cello, which was probably the biggest test of patience I've ever faced. I started when I was twenty-three, which is quite late for a stringed instrument, and I took lessons once a week with a teacher who lived near my office. I'd always loved the sound of the cello, and I think I imagined that within a few months I'd be playing beautiful pieces of music. The reality was very different. For the first few weeks, I could barely produce a clean note. Most of the time the sound was scratchy and unpleasant, and my neighbours must have been delighted. My teacher insisted that I spend ages on very basic exercises, just moving the bow evenly across one string, and I found that incredibly frustrating, because I felt I wasn't getting anywhere. There were several moments when I seriously considered giving up. What helped me stay patient was a couple of things. First, my teacher suggested recording myself once a month. When I listened back to the recordings, I could hear that I was actually improving, even though it didn't feel like it day to day. Second, I stopped practising for long, exhausting sessions and did twenty minutes every day instead, which felt more manageable. And I set myself small goals, like playing one simple piece by the end of the term. After about a year, I was able to play some short pieces reasonably well, and I eventually joined an amateur orchestra. What I learned from the experience is that progress in anything worthwhile is usually much slower and less visible than we expect, and that the trick is to measure it over months rather than days. I've applied that lesson to other things since then, such as learning languages and even getting fit.

topic: A risk that turned out well
cue: Describe a risk you took that turned out well.
bullets: why you decided to take it
closing: and explain how you felt when it turned out well.
followUps: Would you take a similar risk again?
sampleAnswer: The risk I want to describe is when I left a stable job to join a very small start-up. This was about three years ago. At the time, I was working for a large insurance company. The salary was good, the hours were reasonable, and in theory I could have stayed there for the rest of my career. But I was bored. The work was very repetitive, and I felt I wasn't learning anything new. Then a former classmate of mine got in touch. She and two friends had set up a company that develops software to help small farms reduce water use, and they were looking for someone to handle their finances and operations. The offer was exciting but frankly quite scary. The salary was about thirty per cent lower than what I was earning, there was no guarantee the company would still exist in a year, and I'd be giving up a lot of security, like a good pension and private health insurance. A lot of things could have gone wrong. The company could have run out of money, which happens to most start-ups, and I might have found myself unemployed with a gap in my CV. My parents were very worried and kept telling me I was being irresponsible. In the end, I decided to take it because I felt that if I didn't, I'd always wonder what might have happened. I also made sure I had enough savings to survive for six months if everything collapsed, which made the risk feel more manageable. Fortunately, it turned out really well. The company got a significant investment the following year, it's now grown to about forty employees, and I'm in charge of a team. When I realised that it was going to work, I felt a huge sense of relief, but also pride, because I'd trusted my own judgement despite everyone's doubts.

topic: Something you learned from a younger person
cue: Describe a time when you learned something from a child or a younger person.
bullets: how they taught it to you
closing: and explain why this experience was memorable.
followUps: Do you think adults should learn more from children?
sampleAnswer: I'd like to talk about something I learned from my niece, Lucía, when she was about eight years old. It was a couple of summers ago, and I was spending a week at my sister's house by the sea. One afternoon, I was trying to finish some work on my laptop while Lucía was building an enormous sandcastle on the beach. I was stressed, and I kept checking my phone, and at some point she asked me why I looked so worried. I explained that I had a deadline, and she said, very seriously, that I should come and help her for five minutes because it would make me feel better. I went along with it mainly to be polite, but I ended up spending nearly an hour with her. What struck me was the way she approached the whole thing. Every time a wave knocked down part of the castle, I expected her to get upset, but she just laughed and started building it again, sometimes in a completely different shape. When I asked her why she didn't mind, she shrugged and said that the fun part was building it, not having it. I know it sounds like a simple thing for a child to say, but it really stayed with me. I tend to be quite a perfectionist, and I often focus so much on the result that I don't enjoy the process at all, whether it's at work or in my hobbies. What Lucía taught me, without even meaning to, was that it's possible to put a lot of effort into something and still not be devastated when it doesn't turn out as planned. The experience was memorable partly because it was so unexpected. You assume that you, as the adult, are the one who's supposed to teach the child. But that afternoon it was definitely the other way round, and I still think about it whenever I feel myself getting too anxious about the outcome of something.
